blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Divergent boundaries occur where plates separate, allowing magma to rise and form mid-ocean ridges or rift valleys.
Convergent boundaries involve plate collisions, creating volcanic chains, island arcs, or fold mountains depending on the crust types.
Continental–continental collisions at convergent boundaries produce massive fold mountain systems like the Himalayas.
Transform boundaries feature strike-slip faults where accumulated stress release results in earthquakes.

blocks.content: • Magma rises to fill the gap created by separating plates.
• Produces mid-ocean ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Continental–continental collision forms large fold mountains such as the Himalayas.
• On continents, divergence forms rift valleys like the East African Rift.

rows: Plates separate; rising magma forms mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys
Plates collide; forms volcanic chains, island arcs, or fold mountains
Plates slide past each other along strike-slip faults, releasing earthquake stress

blocks.content: • Oceanic–continental convergence forms volcanic mountain chains.
• Continental–continental collision forms large fold mountains such as the Himalayas.

items: Himalayas are a prime example of continental–continental convergent collision frequently asked in physical geography questions.
East African Rift represents a continental divergent boundary, whereas the Mid-Atlantic Ridge represents an oceanic divergent boundary.
San Andreas Fault is the standard example of a transform boundary characterized by strike-slip faulting.

blocks.content: • Earthquakes occur due to sudden release of accumulated stress.
